q-12706:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2}{3}(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{9}+\frac{2{x}^{3}}{27}-\frac{2D}{3} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{27}(9(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{2D}{3}.$

q-8479:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{\pi }{4} & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ 2x & =\frac{5\pi }{12}+n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{n\pi }{2}+\frac{5\pi }{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{24}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{17\pi }{24}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{29\pi }{24}$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x=\frac{41\pi }{24}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=\frac{5\pi }{24},\frac{17\pi }{24},\frac{29\pi }{24},\frac{41\pi }{24}.
$$

Finally, since ${x}_{1}=\frac{5\pi }{24}$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{17\pi }{24},$ we have

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{24}\cdot \frac{17\pi }{24}=\frac{85{\pi }^{2}}{576}.
$$

q-82373:
First, we rearrange the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x-{45}^{∘})-\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x-{45}^{∘}) & =\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2x-{45}^{∘}) & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2x-{45}^{∘}) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{45}^{∘} & ={45}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving our equation for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={45}^{∘}+{45}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ x & ={45}^{∘}+n\cdot {90}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}.$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x={45}^{∘}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x={135}^{∘}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x={225}^{∘}$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x={315}^{∘}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}.$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x={45}^{∘},{135}^{∘},{225}^{∘},{315}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ is $45\cdot 135=6\,075.$

q-77809:
Recall that the range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ for $0\le x<2\pi $ is given by

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

So, the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=k$ has no solutions for $k\in (-1,1).$ 

Therefore, of the given equations, only equations I and III have no solutions.

q-12257:
Let $P$ be the matrix that represents the rotation and let $Q$ be the matrix that represents the stretch. These are given by the following elementary transformation matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{5\pi }{4}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{5\pi }{4}) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{5\pi }{4}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{5\pi }{4})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\ Q & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the combined transformation can be represented by the matrix $QP:$

$$
\begin{aligned}QP & =(\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}])(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{6\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 6 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-48430:
The intermediate value theorem states the following.

*Let $f(x)$ be a function that is **continuous** on a closed interval $[a,b].$ If $k$ is a number that lies between $f(a)$ **and** $f(b)$ **inclusively**, then there exists a number $c\in [a,b]$ such that $f(c)=k.$*

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II".

q-48334:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[-2,3],$ so the intermediate value theorem guarantees that $f(x)=k$ has a solution for each value of $k$ between $f(-2)$ and $f(3)$ inclusively.

Since $f(-2)=6$ and $f(3)=2$, we must have 
$k\in [2,6].$

Therefore, the missing part is "$2$ and $6$".

q-105684:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[1,4],$ therefore, the intermediate value theorem guarantees that $f(x)=k$ has a solution for each value of $k$ between $f(1)$ and $f(4).$

Since $f(1)=2$ and $f(4)=66,$ we must have 
$k\in [2,66].$

Among the given options, only $k=1$ does not belong to the interval $[2,66].$

q-47101:
Since the function $g(x)$ is continuous on $[2,4]$, the intermediate value theorem guarantees that $g(x)=k$ has a solution for each value of $k$ between $g(2)$ and $g(4).$

Since $g(2)=0$ and $g(4)=-12,$ we must have 
$k\in [-12,0].$

Among the given options, only $k=1$ does not belong to the interval $[-12,0].$

q-78542:
Since $g$ is a continuous function on $[-1,2]$, we can apply the intermediate value theorem (IVT) in any subinterval of $[-1,2].$

We will go through each subinterval of $[-1,2]$ and check if the IVT guarantees a solution to the equation $g(x)=1$ on this interval.

- On the subinterval $[-1,1],$ we have $g(-1)=2$ and $g(1)=0.$ Since $1\in [0,2],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[1,2],$ we have $g(1)=0$ and $g(2)=3.$ Since $1\in [0,3],$ the IVT  *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=1$ on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to $g(x)=1$ on the subintervals $[-1,1]$ and $[1,2].$ Therefore, $g(x)=1$ has at least two solutions.

q-105701:
Since $g$ is a continuous function on $[2,7]$, we can apply the intermediate value theorem (IVT) in any subinterval of $[2,7].$

So, we will go through each subinterval of $[2,7]$ and check if the IVT guarantees a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1.$

- On the subinterval $[2,3],$ we have $g(2)=-2$ and $g(3)=1.$ Since $-1\in [-2,1],$  the IVT *does * guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[3,4],$ we have $g(3)=1$ and $g(4)=-3.$ Since $-1\in [-3,1],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[4,5],$ we have $g(4)=-3$ and $g(5)=1.$ Since $-1\in [-3,1],$ the IVT *does * guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[5,6],$ we have $g(5)=1$ and $g(6)=0.$ Since $-1\notin [0,1],$ the IVT does *not* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[6,7],$ we have $g(6)=0$ and $g(7)=2.$ Since $-1\notin [0,2],$ the IVT does *not* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to $g(x)=-1$ on the subintervals $[2,3],$ $[3,4]$  and $[4,5].$ Therefore, $g(x)=-1$ has at least three solutions on $[2,7].$

q-47077:
The intermediate value theorem can be applied to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

The function is discontinuous at $x=1.$ To see this, we note that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x)=2\ne 3={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x).
$$

 

We conclude that the intermediate value theorem can be applied to the function $f(x)$ only on closed intervals that do not contain the point $x=1.$ 

From the given options, only the interval $[-2,0]$ is allowed.  The intervals $(1,3]$ and $[-2,1)$ are not closed, $[-2,1]$ and $[0,3]$ contain the point $x=1.$

q-118090:
Recall the following special limit: 

$$
e={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}
$$

Now, we rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{nxy} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{xy} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{xy} \\  & ={e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

q-118135:
Recall the following special limit: 

$$
{e}^{x}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{x}{n})}^{n}
$$

Now, we rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{x}{n})}^{n{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{x}{n})}^{n}]}^{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{x}{n})}^{n}]}^{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={({e}^{x})}^{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{x{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
